lessons.title: Case Study: Scoring Two Companies Side by Side

body.text: Two companies in the same industry, at the same multiple, with almost the same profit. The scorecard is the only thing that tells them apart, and it tells them apart completely.

children.text: This lesson runs the 20-point checklist end to end on two fictional specialty chemicals companies built from the patterns you have seen throughout this course. Vasant Chemicals and Kaveri Speciality are both mid caps listed on NSE, both around ₹9,700 crore of market value, both earning about ₹400 crore, both trading at roughly 24 times earnings. On a screener, they look like the same stock.

body.text: Both companies are fictional, but every individual finding below is drawn from the real cases in this course: falling promoter stakes, rising pledges, related party distributors, family payrolls, capitalised costs, and regulatory files. Recognising these in combination is the whole skill.

body.caption: Checks 1 to 5, with the evidence behind each score

cells: 1. Promoter holding and trend
52%, share count unchanged for five years
47%, down from 54% through small open market sales every year, unexplained
2. Pledge
Nil
38% of promoter holding, up from 9% in three years
3. Group structure
Four subsidiaries, one in Germany where it sells
23 subsidiaries including four in Mauritius and Singapore; consolidated profit below standalone for three years
4. Promoter group pressure
No material debt outside the listed company
Unlisted realty arm with rated debt; rating rationale flags refinancing risk
5. Changes in control
QIP at a 3% discount to institutions, no promoter allotment
Warrants to promoters at the floor price proposed this year
Section A subtotal

body.caption: Checks 6 to 10, with the evidence behind each score

cells: 6. Board composition
Eight directors, five independent, non-executive independent chair
Seven directors, four classified independent, promoter is executive chair
7. Real independence
One director in year nine; others mid-tenure with sector expertise
A former CFO, a lawyer whose firm advises the promoter family, and a director in year nine sitting on four group boards
8. Audit committee
Chaired by a chartered accountant, fully independent
Made up of exactly those three weakest directors, chaired by the former CFO
9. Audit opinion and CARO
Unmodified; Key Audit Matter on inventory valuation; clean CARO
Unmodified; Key Audit Matter on recoverability of advances; CARO 3(iii) reports ₹210 crore of related party loans with no repayment schedule
10. Auditor changes
Scheduled rotation in FY24 to another large firm
Large firm resigned mid-term in FY24 citing pre-occupation; company cited a fee dispute; replaced by a much smaller firm
Section B subtotal

body.text: Look closely at check 10 for Kaveri. The auditor gave a soft reason, so this is not the red line from Lesson 21, which requires the auditor to cite missing information or unresolved concerns. It still scores zero, because a large firm leaving mid-term, a company explanation that contradicts the auditor's, and a much smaller replacement is the pattern from Lesson 11. Judgement still matters; the checklist organises it, it does not replace it.

body.caption: Checks 11 to 15, with the evidence behind each score

cells: 11. Managerial pay
MD paid ₹6.2 crore, 1.5% of profit, 62 times median pay; pay growing 9% a year against profit growth of 14%
Three family executives paid ₹31 crore together, 7.75% of profit, each on a 2% profit commission; pay growing 19% a year against profit growth of 8%
12. Related party purchases and sales
Only with wholly owned subsidiaries, plus ₹1.1 crore of promoter rent unchanged for five years
19% of revenue sold through a promoter-owned distributor that pays in 138 days against 71 days for other customers; 14% of raw materials bought from a promoter entity
13. Related party loans and guarantees
₹180 crore guarantee for the wholly owned German subsidiary, 7.8% of net worth
₹210 crore of loans plus ₹190 crore of guarantees to promoter entities, ₹400 crore or 21% of net worth
14. Royalty and brand fees
None
Brand fee to the promoter holding company raised from 0.5% to 1.5% of revenue
15. Cash returned and where cash sits
28% of profit and 65% of free cash flow paid out; ₹430 crore of cash with a disclosed capex plan
9% payout; ₹620 crore of cash and investments, of which ₹260 crore is deposits with group companies
Section C subtotal

children.text: Section D: Stewardship, Numbers and Conduct

body.caption: Checks 16 to 20, with the evidence behind each score

cells: 16. Incremental ROCE and value per rupee retained
Incremental ROCE 21% against a 22% average; ₹2.30 of value created per rupee retained
Incremental ROCE 9% against a 17% average; ₹0.70 per rupee retained
17. Acquisitions and diversification
Two bolt-on deals totalling ₹210 crore in the core business, no impairment
₹380 crore spent including a hospitality venture, with ₹120 crore already written off
18. Earnings quality
Cash conversion averaging 0.84; debtor days improved from 62 to 58; no exceptional items in five years
Cash conversion down from 0.78 to 0.39; debtor days up from 71 to 119; ₹90 crore of development cost capitalised each year; exceptional items in four of five years
19. Guidance versus delivery
Margin target met in three of four years; capex of ₹600 crore promised and ₹640 crore spent
Guided 20% growth three years running and delivered 9%, 11%, and 12%; ₹300 crore of a ₹500 crore QIP still unspent after two years
20. Regulatory footprint and votes
One late filing fine of ₹1.2 lakh in FY23; 96% institutional support at the last AGM
Fines in four of five years; a SEBI adjudication order naming the promoters over delayed encumbrance disclosure; 41% of institutional votes against the MD's reappointment
Section D subtotal

children.text: The Red Line Test Comes First

Run Kaveri against the five red lines from Lesson 21. The audit opinion is unmodified, so no. The auditor resigned citing pre-occupation rather than missing evidence, so no. No regulator has restrained the promoters from boards, only penalised them, so no. Related party exposure is ₹400 crore against ₹1,900 crore of net worth, which is 21%, below the 25% line. The pledge is 38%, below half the promoter holding. Not one red line is crossed, and the answer is still a clear no, because a score of 8 out of 40 is what twenty separate small concessions look like when you add them up.

body.title: Cash flow from operations as a share of EBITDA

children.text: The scorecard says avoid. The valuation makes the point in rupees. Adjust Kaveri's ₹400 crore of reported profit for three things you found: ₹90 crore of development cost capitalised each year, exceptional items averaging ₹40 crore a year that recur, and ₹25 crore of interest accrued on related party loans that is not being received in cash. Tax each adjustment at 25%.

body.title: Adjust the Earnings
body.prompt: Starting from ₹400 crore of reported profit, subtract the after-tax effect of ₹90 crore of capitalised development cost, ₹40 crore of recurring exceptional items, and ₹25 crore of accrued but uncollected related party interest, using a 25% tax rate. What is the adjusted profit, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Each adjustment costs 75% of its value after tax: ₹67.5 crore, ₹30 crore, and ₹18.75 crore, totalling ₹116.25 crore. ₹400 crore minus ₹116.25 crore is ₹283.75 crore. At an unchanged market value of ₹9,600 crore, Kaveri is not trading at 24 times earnings. It is trading at about 34 times the earnings you can actually believe in, while Vasant trades at 24 times earnings that convert into cash.

body.title: What Each Score Actually Means for You

columns.label: Vasant at 36
points: Reported profit is close to economic profit, so the P/E means what it says
Remaining risks are operational: demand, input costs, execution
Watch list is short: the independent director in year nine, and the German subsidiary guarantee
Normal position size, annual rescore, alerts for material events

columns.label: Kaveri at 8
points: Reported profit is materially overstated relative to cash
Value is leaking to promoter entities through pricing, credit, loans, brand fees, and pay
A rising pledge means a promoter who needs cash, and the listed company is the nearest source
No position size is appropriate until the pattern reverses and stays reversed

body.title: Where Did Kaveri Lose the Most?
body.question: Kaveri scored 3, 2, 2, and 1 across Sections A to D. Which section's weakness tells you most directly that cash is leaving the company for the promoter's benefit?
options: Section D, stewardship, numbers and conduct
body.explanation: Section C is where money physically moves: related party sales and purchases, loans and guarantees, royalty, pay, and payouts. Section A explains the motive, Section B explains why nobody stopped it, and Section D shows the consequences in the numbers and the regulatory file. Read them together, but Section C is the one that measures the leak.

body.title: Kaveri Falls 40%
body.scenario: Nine months later, Kaveri Speciality has fallen 40% and now trades at about 14 times reported earnings, a large discount to Vasant and to the sector. Nothing in the governance file has improved: the pledge is now 44%, the related party distributor still owes 141 days of sales, and the promoter warrants have been issued at the floor price. A brokerage note calls it 'deep value with a governance overhang that is now more than priced in'. A friend asks whether the fall has made it cheap.
body.prompt: Has it? What specific, verifiable changes would make you reconsider?
body.modelAnswer: No, and the earnings adjustment shows why. On adjusted profit of roughly ₹284 crore, a 40% lower market value of about ₹5,760 crore is still around 20 times believable earnings, not 14 times, and that is before any provision against the ₹400 crore of related party exposure, which is 21% of net worth. Meanwhile the governance position has worsened, not improved: a higher pledge, unchanged collection from the promoter distributor, and warrants issued at a floor price that let the promoter increase control cheaply after the fall. A discount is only an opportunity when the cause of the discount is temporary and you can name what would end it. Here the specific, checkable changes would be: related party loans and deposits repaid in cash and confirmed in the next related party note, receivable days from the distributor falling towards the company average, the pledge falling back below 10%, cash conversion recovering above 0.7 for two consecutive years, a credible auditor issuing an unmodified opinion after a full year, and no new regulatory action. Until several of those are visible in filings rather than promised on a concall, the stock is cheap for a reason that is still operating.

body.title: Do This With Two Real Companies
steps: Pick two listed companies in the same industry with similar size and valuation, one you own and one you do not
Score both on all 20 checks in the same sitting, writing one line of evidence and the source document for each
Run the five red lines on both before comparing totals
Compare section subtotals, not just totals, and note where each company loses points
Adjust reported profit for anything you found in Section D, then recompute the P/E you are actually paying
Write the specific, verifiable changes that would raise the weaker company's score, and diarise a check in six months
Keep both scorecards; next year, the direction of travel is as informative as the level

body.text: Vasant Chemicals and Kaveri Speciality are fictional companies created for teaching, and any resemblance to a real company is coincidental. The scoring framework is educational and is not a rating methodology or investment advice.

points: Two companies with the same sector, size, profit, and P/E can score 36 and 8 on governance, and the market often charges the same price for both
Kaveri crossed none of the five red lines and was still a clear avoid, because twenty small concessions add up to the same conclusion
Section subtotals matter: Section A explains the motive, Section B why nobody stopped it, Section C where cash actually leaves, and Section D the consequences
Adjusting for capitalised costs, recurring exceptional items, and accrued but uncollected interest turned a reported ₹400 crore profit into ₹283.75 crore, and a 24 P/E into about 34
A falling share price does not fix governance; a discount is only an opportunity if you can name the specific, verifiable changes that would end it
Always score a comparable company alongside, so your judgement is relative to a real alternative rather than to a story
